body.text: The central challenge is to reconcile the competing political economies of energy transition, address the persistent deficit in climate finance, and restore confidence in multilateral institution

The collapse of the COP31 climate summit in Antalya, Turkey, represents a significant setback for international climate diplomacy. For the first time since the Copenhagen summit of 2009, a major UN climate conference has concluded without adopting its overarching political agreement.

The failure is particularly consequential given that the negotiations extended nearly two days beyond their scheduled conclusion, making COP31 the longest climate summit on record. What was expected to reaffirm the international community’s collective commitment to climate action instead exposed the widening fault lines within the global climate regime.

At the heart of the impasse was an increasingly familiar but politically consequential question: the future of fossil fuels. The inability to agree on an explicit reference to coal, oil and gas, or to establish a pathway for transitioning away from them, revealed the limits of climate multilateralism when confronted with entrenched economic and strategic interests.

Saudi Arabia, other OPEC members and Russia resisted language that could have committed countries to a more definitive fossil-fuel transition. Their preference was for a formulation centred on carbon capture and other technological solutions, rather than an explicit acknowledgement of the need to move away from fossil-fuel dependence.

The resulting draft was revealing in its omissions. It avoided direct references to fossil fuels, coal and oil, offering instead an indirect allusion to the commitment made at COP28 in Dubai in 2023 to transition away from fossil fuels in energy systems. The reluctance to reaffirm or strengthen that commitment was not merely a drafting disagreement. It reflected a deeper contest over the distributional consequences of decarbonisation and the extent to which climate action should constrain the economic choices of fossil-fuel-producing states.

The European Union, alongside the United Kingdom, Norway, Panama, the Marshall Islands, Vanuatu and Belize, refused to endorse what they regarded as an inadequate and politically diluted outcome. Approximately 130 countries had supported stronger language on fossil fuels. The European delegation’s walkout during the closing plenary underscored the extent of the diplomatic rupture.
COP31 President Murat Kurum and negotiations chair Chris Bowen ultimately acknowledged that consensus was unattainable and refrained from formally adopting the proposed decision.

The failure of COP31 cannot be attributed exclusively to the politics of fossil fuels. The persistent inadequacy of climate finance commitments constituted another important source of discontent. Developing countries and climate-vulnerable states had sought more substantial and predictable adaptation financing, with earlier negotiating proposals contemplating a threefold increase in annual support to approximately $120 billion by 2035. The absence of concrete financial targets, credible baselines and enforceable commitments in the final text reinforced longstanding concerns that the burden of climate action continues to fall disproportionately on countries with the least historical responsibility for global emissions.

The absence of the United States as an effective diplomatic interlocutor further complicated the negotiations. Under the Trump administration, Washington did not send an official delegation, reflecting its wider retreat from the international climate process.

This absence was significant not simply because of America’s economic and emissions profile, but also because Washington has historically played an important role in brokering compromises between developed and developing economies, often in conjunction with China. Its disengagement created an additional diplomatic vacuum at a moment when the negotiations required precisely the kind of political intervention that could have helped bridge competing positions.

The broader geopolitical environment was hardly conducive to compromise. Strategic rivalries, declining trust in multilateral institutions and competing national priorities have increasingly complicated international cooperation on climate change. The criticism directed at the Turkish-Australian co-presidency’s management of the final negotiating phase reflected a wider frustration with the inability of the COP process to translate political declarations into meaningful collective action.

UN Secretary-General António Guterres, meanwhile, pointed to the influence of powerful fossil-fuel interests in obstructing progress. His intervention captured a central contradiction of contemporary climate diplomacy: the institutions tasked with managing the transition away from carbon-intensive development remain deeply exposed to the political and economic interests invested in its continuation.

There is also a structural problem with the UN climate negotiating architecture. The consensus-based decision-making framework of the UN Framework Convention on Climate Change allows individual countries or relatively small groups of states to prevent the adoption of ambitious agreements. While consensus is intended to preserve the legitimacy and inclusiveness of multilateral decision-making, it can also produce outcomes shaped by the lowest common denominator. COP31 has once again raised questions about whether a negotiating system designed to accommodate divergent national interests can deliver the speed and ambition demanded by the climate emergency.

The collapse of the overarching political agreement does not mean that COP31 produced no outcomes. Negotiators managed to advance certain technical decisions relating to just transition, electrification and funding arrangements. Nor does the failure invalidate previous commitments, including the COP28 language on transitioning away from fossil fuels. Nevertheless, these incremental achievements are unlikely to compensate for the political damage caused by the inability to secure a common declaration.

The significance of Antalya therefore extends beyond the immediate failure of a negotiating text. The summit has exposed the growing divergence between countries that view the fossil-fuel transition as indispensable to the credibility of global climate action and those that regard such commitments as a threat to their economic and strategic interests. It has also brought into sharper focus the unresolved question of climate justice: whether developed economies are prepared to provide the financial and technological support necessary to make the transition politically and economically viable for the developing world.

COP31 illustrates a troubling paradox at the heart of global climate governance. The urgency of collective action has never been greater, yet the political foundations for achieving it appear increasingly fragile. The 1.5°C threshold is under mounting pressure, climate impacts are intensifying, and the space for incrementalism is narrowing. Even as the scientific case for accelerated decarbonisation becomes more compelling, geopolitical competition and domestic economic considerations continue to obstruct agreement.

The central challenge is no longer simply to negotiate more ambitious climate targets. It is to reconcile the competing political economies of energy transition, address the persistent deficit in climate finance, and restore confidence in multilateral institutions.

The Antalya summit may consequently be remembered less for what it failed to adopt than for what it revealed about the changing character of climate multilateralism. The central challenge is no longer simply to negotiate more ambitious climate targets. It is to reconcile the competing political economies of energy transition, address the persistent deficit in climate finance, and restore confidence in multilateral institutions. Without such a recalibration, future COPs risk becoming exercises in managing diplomatic disagreements rather than instruments for delivering meaningful climate action.
This commentary originally appeared in Moneycontrol.
